title: IB Business Management Common Mistakes to Avoid
summary: IB Business Management common mistakes explained, from misreading command terms to missing evidence, units and timing, with practical fixes for exams.
body_markdown:
A student leaves an IB Business Management exam feeling strangely confident. The definitions were familiar. The calculations looked manageable. Every page contained an answer.


Then the marked script returns. One response explained when it should have evaluated. A profitability ratio had no percentage sign. An argument about expansion never referred to the business in the stimulus. The final question ended halfway through a sentence.


This student is hypothetical, but the pattern is familiar. Many **IB Business Management common mistakes** are not failures of knowledge. They are failures of execution: answering the wrong task, leaving evidence unused, presenting incomplete calculations, or allocating time badly.


The good news is that execution can be trained.


### The quick exam checklist


Before moving to the next question, ask:


- Did I follow the command term?
- Did I answer the precise question, not merely write about the topic?
- Did I use specific evidence from the stimulus?
- Did I show my calculation stages and include the correct unit?
- Did I develop both sides where evaluation is required?
- Am I spending time in proportion to the available marks?


For a broader preparation framework, read RevisionDojo's guide on[how to get a 7 in IB Business Management](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-get-a-7-in-ib-business-management) .


### Mistake: misreading the command term


The hypothetical student saw “evaluate” and wrote three advantages of external growth. The knowledge was accurate, but the answer did not weigh strengths against limitations or reach a supported judgment.


The IB Business Management guide explains that command terms indicate the depth required. “Explain” requires reasons or causes. “Discuss” asks for a considered, balanced review. “Evaluate” requires an appraisal that weighs strengths and limitations. Treating these words as interchangeable changes the task you are answering.


### The fix: translate the instruction before writing


Pause and convert the command term into an answer shape:


Command term Practical response shape


Define Give the precise meaning


Explain Make a point, then develop why or how it occurs


Analyse Break the issue into relevant relationships and consequences


Discuss Consider different arguments and support them with evidence


Evaluate Weigh strengths and limitations, then reach a contextual judgment


Recommend Select an option and justify why it best fits the organization


Underline the command term and the object of the question. “Evaluate one source of finance for Company X” is narrower than “evaluate sources of finance.” That difference protects you from producing a polished answer to a question that was never asked.


Use the[IB exam command terms list](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-exam-command-terms-list) as a reference, then learn[how to use command terms effectively](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-use-command-terms-effectively-in-ib-exams) under timed conditions.


### Mistake: writing theory without case evidence


A student may know that democratic leadership can improve motivation. That is subject knowledge. To earn stronger application and analysis marks, the response must connect the idea to the organization, its employees, its objectives, or another relevant detail from the stimulus.


Weak application simply repeats a company name: “This would motivate employees at Zeta Ltd.” Stronger application uses evidence and explains its significance: “Because Zeta Ltd's experienced designers currently have little input into product decisions, consultation may improve motivation and generate ideas that senior managers lack.”


The evidence is doing analytical work. It is not decoration.


### The fix: use an evidence chain


Build analytical paragraphs with four moves:


1. Make a relevant business point.
2. Select a precise fact from the stimulus.
3. Explain the resulting consequence for the organization.
4. Link that consequence back to the question.


For evaluative responses, add a limitation or condition. A recommendation that suits a cash-rich multinational may be unrealistic for a small business facing a liquidity problem. Context changes the quality of a decision.


This aligns with the official markband emphasis on relevant tools and theories, substantiated arguments, balance, and stimulus application. RevisionDojo's[Business Management exam score guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-maximize-your-score-in-ib-business-management) provides further strategies for turning knowledge into case-specific analysis.


### Mistake: losing calculation marks through presentation


Our hypothetical student calculated a profit margin of 12 but omitted the percent sign. Elsewhere, the correct answer appeared without working. These errors feel small because the mathematical thinking may be sound. In an exam, however, the written response is the only evidence a marker can assess.


A student detective questions a missing percent sign beside an exam calculation


### The fix: make every calculation auditable


Use a repeatable sequence:


- Write the formula.
- Substitute the values.
- Show the calculation.
- State the answer with its unit.
- Interpret the result if the question requests analysis or comment.


For example:


Profit margin=profit before interest and taxsales revenue×100\\text{Profit margin}=\\frac{\\text{profit before interest and tax}}{\\text{sales revenue}}\\times 100

A result might require a percentage, currency amount, number of days, or ratio. Read the data carefully because figures may be presented in thousands or millions. Keep sufficient calculator precision during the working and round only the final answer unless the question specifies otherwise.


The official guide defines “calculate” as obtaining a numerical answer while showing relevant stages. That makes visible working part of the response, not optional rough work.


### Mistake: spending too long on early questions


Some students write everything they know for a low-mark question, then rush the extended response where judgment and synthesis matter. The problem is not effort. It is capital allocation, which is fitting for a Business Management exam.


According to the current course structure, Paper 1 lasts 1 hour 30 minutes for both SL and HL. Paper 2 lasts 1 hour 30 minutes at SL and 1 hour 45 minutes at HL. HL Paper 3 lasts 1 hour 15 minutes. Knowing the duration is useful, but timing improves only when it becomes a practised decision.


### The fix: budget time by marks


At the start, note the marks available and establish a rough time allowance per mark, while reserving a few minutes for checking. If time expires, leave space and continue. An unfinished high-value response usually costs more than an imperfect sentence earlier in the paper.


Checking time should have specific jobs:


- Add missing units and labels.
- Confirm that each response follows its command term.
- Check that evaluative answers contain a judgment.
- Look for unused stimulus evidence.
- Verify that every required question has been attempted.


Follow the approach in RevisionDojo's[Business Management mock exam preparation guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-business-management-mock-exam-prep-november) . Timed practice reveals habits that ordinary revision hides.


### Turn avoidable mistakes into a training system


Reading more notes is not always the answer. If your weakness is execution, your revision must reproduce the decisions made under exam pressure.


Use RevisionDojo's[complete IB Business Management coverage](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-ib-business-management-coverage) to diagnose gaps with Study Notes and Flashcards. Then move into the Questionbank, where you can practise one command term or topic repeatedly. Use AI Chat when a concept remains unclear, and Grading tools to inspect whether your analysis actually answers the task.


As the exam approaches, use Predicted Papers and Mock Exams to combine recall, calculations, evidence and timing. Most importantly, **practise in the Questionbank and sit timed papers in Exam mode** . That is where knowing becomes doing.


Easy marks are rarely easy because they require no knowledge. They are easy because the student already has the knowledge and needs a reliable process for showing it. RevisionDojo helps build that process, one answer at a time.
